title: Āpo vā idaṃ sarvam: all this is water
theme: A litany identifying the waters with everything — beings, breath, food, the cosmic sovereign, the Veda, truth, the gods and the three worlds — closed by Om.

words.context: Sāyaṇa: «यदिदं जगदस्ति तत्सर्वमापो वै जलमेव» — whatever this world is, all of it is water

words.gram: n. nom. pl., Vedic form (classical viśvāni)

words.context: Sāyaṇa: «विश्वा भूतानि सर्वाणि प्राणिशरीराण्यापो जलं रेतोरूपेण तदुत्पादकत्वात्» — all living bodies, since water as seed produces them; Bhāskara: «भूतानि पृथिव्यादीनि» — the elements, earth and the rest
Sāyaṇa: «उदपानेन प्राणानामाप्यायनात्» — because drinking water nourishes them
Sāyaṇa: «क्षीरस्वरूपेण तत्र परिणतत्वात्» — because water is transformed in them into milk
Sāyaṇa: «जलस्यान्नहेतुत्वं प्रसिद्धम्» — that water is the cause of food is well known
Sāyaṇa: «अमृतं देवैरूपजीव्यं वस्त्वापः» — the substance the gods live on; Bhāskara: «अमृतम् आत्मा» — the self
Sāyaṇa: «सम्यग्राजत इति सूत्रात्मा हिरण्यगर्भः सम्राट्» — shining fully: Hiraṇyagarbha, the thread-self
Sāyaṇa: «विस्पष्टं राजत इति ब्रह्माण्डदेहः पुरुषो विराट्» — the person whose body is the cosmic egg
Sāyaṇa: «इन्द्रियादिनैरपेक्ष्येण स्वयमेव राजत इत्यव्याकृताभिमानीश्वरः स्वराट्» — shining of himself, without senses: the lord who identifies with the unmanifest

words.gram: n. nom. pl., in the recitation text’s spelling (classical chandāṃsi)
words.context: Sāyaṇa: «छन्दांसि गायत्र्यादीनि» — gāyatrī and the others

words.gram: n. nom. pl., in the recitation text’s spelling (classical jyotīṃṣi)
words.context: Sāyaṇa: «ज्योतींष्यादित्यादीनि» — the sun and the other lights

words.gram: n. nom. pl., in the recitation text’s spelling (classical yajūṃṣi)
words.context: Sāyaṇa: «यजूंष्यनियताक्षरा मन्त्राः» — mantras without a fixed number of syllables
Sāyaṇa: «सत्यं यथार्थकथनम्» — speaking what is so; Bhāskara: «सत्यं ब्रह्म प्रपञ्चोत्तीर्णं» — Brahman beyond the world
Sāyaṇa: «सर्वा देवता इन्द्रादयः» — Indra and the others
Sāyaṇa: «भूर्भुवः स्वस्त्रयो लोकाः» — the three worlds

The anonymous commentator: «एताश्चाऽऽपो मूलकारणपरमात्मरूपेण प्रणवप्रतिपाद्या इति वक्तुमोंकारः पठितः» — Om is recited to say that these waters, as the supreme self, the root cause, are what the praṇava means

sandhi.type: -aḥ before v; ai before a vowel
sandhi.rule: āpaḥ + vai → āpo vai; vai + idam: ai becomes āy before a vowel (P. 6.1.78 (एचोऽयवायावः)) and the y is dropped (P. 8.3.19 (लोपः शाकल्यस्य)): vā idam.

sandhi.type: -aḥ before a vowel other than a
sandhi.rule: paśavaḥ + āpaḥ → paśava āpaḥ: the visarga becomes y and the y is dropped (P. 8.3.17 (भोभगोअघोअपूर्वस्य योऽशि), P. 8.3.19 (लोपः शाकल्यस्य)).

sandhi.type: -aḥ before a; final m before a vowel
sandhi.rule: āpaḥ + annam → āpo ’nnam, the a elided (P. 6.1.109 (एङः पदान्तादति)); annam āpaḥ, with the m joined to the vowel.
A final ṭ becomes ḍ before a vowel (P. 8.2.39 (झलां जशोऽन्ते)): samrāḍ āpaḥ.

sandhi.type: visarga before ch; i before a vowel
sandhi.rule: The visarga becomes ś before ch (P. 8.3.34 (विसर्जनीयस्य सः), P. 8.4.40 (स्तोः श्चुना श्चुः)): āpaś chandāṃsi; the recitation text writes the anusvāra before s as ग् (chandāgsi); chandāṃsi + āpaḥ → chandāṃsy āpaḥ.

sandhi.type: suvaḥ before a vowel; -aḥ before o
sandhi.rule: suvaḥ, whose final is r, keeps it before a vowel: suvar āpaḥ; āpaḥ + om → āpa om, the visarga dropped before the vowel.

morphology.note: The Vedic neuter plural in -ā, for classical viśvāni; Bhāskara glosses «विश्वा विश्वानि».

The Taittirīya recitation writes the anusvāra before a sibilant as ग् (chandāgsi, jyotīgṣi, yajūgṣi). The word is chandāṃsi; the padaccheda keeps the recitation text’s own spelling so that it rejoins to the text as printed.
From samrāj, as virāj and svarāj: the final j becomes ṭ in the pausal form and ḍ before the following vowel.

translation.literal: Water, truly, [is] all this; all beings [are] water; the breaths, truly, [are] water; cattle [are] water; food [is] water; the immortal [is] water; the sovereign [is] water; the widely shining [is] water; the self-shining [is] water; the metres [are] water; the lights [are] water; the yajus formulas [are] water; truth [is] water; all the deities [are] water; earth, middle region, heaven [are] water. Om.
translation.readable: All this is water. Water is every being; water is breath; water is cattle, food and the undying. Water is the sovereign, the widely shining and the self-shining. Water is the metres, the lights and the sacred formulas; water is truth; water is all the gods. Earth, sky and heaven are water. Om.

syntax: A chain of nominal identifications without a verb, each pairing āpaḥ (‘the waters’) with one thing: first āpo vai idaṃ sarvam (‘water, truly, is all this’), then one item after another, each with its āpaḥ, ending with the three worlds bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ and Om.

ambiguities.note: The anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa give a reason for each identification — water as the seed of bodies, as what nourishes breath, as milk in cattle, as the cause of food. Bhāskara gives one reason for all: everything depends on water, «सर्वमाप एव तदधीनत्वात्».

metre.name: prose
metre.note: A prose litany of 73 syllables in one line.

beginner: This passage is a hymn to water. Its first words say: all this is water. Then it goes through the world one item at a time and calls each one water: every living being, the breath, cattle, food, the undying, three names of the cosmic ruler, the metres and formulas of the Veda, truth, all the gods, and finally the three worlds — earth, sky and heaven. It ends with Om. The commentators explain each step: bodies come from seed, breath is refreshed by drinking, cattle turn water into milk, rain makes food grow. They also say why the hymn stands here: it is a prayer to the waters to turn away the hardships of drought. One commentator reads the whole as praise of the highest reality under the name of water. The text praises; it makes no promise.
analogy: Like tracing every dish on a table back to the same rain that fell on the fields.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: That water is all this; and then that water is each of a long list — beings, breaths, cattle, food, the immortal, the sovereign, the widely and the self-shining, the metres, the lights, the yajus formulas, truth, all the deities, and the three worlds — closing with Om.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa call it a mantra to the waters that helps by warding off the troubles that come when rain fails: «वृष्ट्यभावकृतोपद्रवपरिहारेणोपकारिणमब्देवताकं मन्त्रमाह». Bhāskara reads it as praise of Brahman as water, «आपो वा इत्यादिनाऽप्त्वेन ब्रह्म स्तूयते», concluding ‘therefore let us worship them’, «तस्मात्ता उपास्मह इति शेषः».

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Sāyaṇa: because drinking nourishes the breaths, and he cites the Chāndogya, introducing it as what the Chāndogya reciters teach: «अत एव च्छन्दोगा आमनन्ति».

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator: Om is recited to show that the waters, as the supreme self, the root cause, are what the praṇava names: «एताश्चाऽऽपो मूलकारणपरमात्मरूपेण प्रणवप्रतिपाद्या इति वक्तुमोंकारः पठितः». Bhāskara takes Om as the supreme self among the things named as water: «ओं परमात्मा आप एव».

schools.disagreement: No Vedānta-school commentary on this anuvāka is in the edition’s sources (Raṅgarāmānuja’s commentary on the Mahānārāyaṇa is not available here). The anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa read a mantra to the waters against drought; Bhāskara reads praise of Brahman as water.

parallels.note: Sāyaṇa supports ‘the breaths are water’ with this passage: ‘breath is made of water; it will not be cut off for one who drinks’.
The Chāndogya likewise calls the earth, the sky, the mountains, gods and humans, cattle and birds ‘water in solid form’.
In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka, ‘in the beginning this was water’, and the waters bring forth truth.

contemporary.text: The litany follows water into everything: bodies, breath, milk, food, the gods themselves. Its commentators read it as a prayer against drought. A list that traces so much back to one resource is a sober reminder of how much depends on it. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: Pick three items from the list. How would you explain, in your own words, that each one ‘is water’?
reflect.deeper: The commentators give either a separate reason for each identification or one reason for all (dependence). Which kind of explanation suits a litany better?
reflect.practice: Notice every use of water in one ordinary day, from waking to sleep.

references.text: Sāyaṇa comments on this anuvāka as his anuvāka 22 (the concordance maps it correctly); the anonymous commentator repeats him nearly word for word. Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara’s comment is his anuvāka 22; the edition’s concordance gives no Bhāskara anuvāka for 10.29, so it is cited here by his own number.

flags.note: The Ānandāśrama pariśiṣṭa text prints chandāsyāpo and jyotīṣyāpo without any mark for the anusvāra, where the base writes ग् and the Tirupati e-text ꣳ; the collation lists these for review.
Concordance: Bhāskara’s anuvāka 22 comments on this anuvāka, but the edition’s map lists nothing for 10.29.
